title: Lethal Mutations
author: Haili Hughes
summary: In this guest piece for Jamie Clark's DistillED newsletter, Haili Hughes explains lethal mutations: changes to an evidence-informed practice that keep its name and look but remove the part that made it support learning. Using mini whiteboards, retrieval Do Nows and the "three comments in every book" version of feedback as examples, she shows how a technique can survive as a routine while its link to responsive teaching disappears. She draws on Jones and Wiliam, Agarwal and colleagues on retrieval, and EEF guidance on feedback and implementation to argue that a school can wrongly conclude a strategy does not work when it has really evaluated a distorted version. She names the causes as compression of ideas on the way from research to policy, leaders asking for observable proxies, and teachers adapting without support. Her five prevention steps are to name the learning purpose, identify what must be preserved, model decisions and rehearse responses, adapt with an explicit reason, and review what students actually learned. She closes by urging schools to make it professionally safe to say a routine has drifted.
points: A lethal mutation is not any adaptation or unfamiliar style but a consequential change in which the activity continues while its learning function weakens.
If a school mandates a distorted version of retrieval practice and then judges retrieval a failure, it has evaluated something other than the process it meant to introduce.
Leaders often ask for something observable, such as three comments per book, because the underlying learning process is harder to judge, and the visible quantity becomes the measure of success.

The five-step prevention routine centres on stating the purpose, protecting the essential features, rehearsing responses to student thinking, justifying adaptations and checking what students learned.
Improvement needs professional safety, because if admitting that a routine has drifted feels like confessing incompetence, people keep performing the routine.
quotes: At its core, a lethal mutation is a change to an evidence-informed practice that undermines how it is supposed to support learning. The activity may retain its original name and appearance, even though its educational value has been weakened or removed.
The routine survives, but its connection to responsive teaching has disappeared. Buying the equipment was the easy part, but knowing what to do with the answers was always the work.
If the school then concludes that retrieval has made little difference, it has evaluated something other than the process it intended to introduce.

Teachers comply, students turn the page, and the visible quantity of feedback becomes the measure of success. Meanwhile, the more revealing questions go unanswered: did students understand the guidance, act on it and improve their work?

Sometimes leaders ask for something observable because the underlying learning process is harder to judge. Sometimes teachers make sensible attempts to manage workload or meet students’ needs, without enough support to recognise which changes might compromise the approach.
A polished demonstration can conceal exactly the knowledge a novice needs to develop.
Look beyond whether the technique happened. Examine responses, subsequent work and remaining errors, then decide whether to retain, refine or reconsider the approach.
Finally, make it professionally safe to say that something has drifted. If acknowledging a problem feels like confessing incompetence, people have a reason to keep performing the routine.
